title: A Joker
text:
It was the New Year’s explosion: chaos of mud and snow, crossed by a thousand carriages, glittering with toys and sweets, swarming with greed and despair; the official delirium of a great city, contrived to trouble the brain of the strongest recluse.

Through all that bustle and din, a donkey trotted briskly, driven by a lout brandishing a whip.

Just as the donkey was about to turn the corner, a young gentleman, gloved, patent-leathered, cruelly cravatted and imprisoned in a new suit, bowed ceremoniously to the humble animal and, taking off his hat, said: “I wish you a good and happy New Year!” Then he turned with a smug air toward some companions or other, as if inviting them to add their approval to his delight.

Without seeing the joker, the donkey kept running zealously toward the place where duty called him.

I was suddenly seized by an immeasurable rage against that magnificent imbecile, who seemed to me to concentrate in himself all the wit of France.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The prose-poem form and its final satirical reversal are preserved.

title: The Soul of Wine
text:
One night the soul of wine sang in the bottles:
“Man, dear castaway, I raise to you
from my glass prison and my crimson seals
a brotherly song filled with light!

I know how one must toil and sweat
upon the burning hillside beneath a scorching sun
to engender my life and give me soul;
but I shall not be ungrateful or cruel to you.

I feel immense delight when I descend
into the mouth of a man exhausted by his work,
and his warm breast is a sweet tomb
that pleases me more than my cool cellars.

Do you hear the Sunday songs resound,
and hope warble in my panting breast?
Elbows on the table, sleeves rolled bare,
you will sing my praises and be happy;

I shall kindle the eyes of your delighted wife;
I shall restore your son’s strength and color,
becoming for that frail athlete of life
the oil that burnishes a wrestler’s muscles.

And I shall fall into you, vegetal ambrosia,
rare grain cast by the eternal Sower,
so that from our love poetry may be born
and rise toward God like a rare flower!”
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The wine’s first-person address and sacred imagery are retained.

title: To One Who Is Too Gay
text:
Your head, your gesture, your air
are lovely as a lovely landscape;
laughter plays across your face
like a fresh wind in a clear sky.

The sorrowful passerby you brush
is dazzled by the health
that springs like radiance
from your shoulders and your arms.

The riotous colors
you scatter over your clothes
make poets dream
of a lively ballet of flowers.

Your mad dresses are the emblem
of your motley spirit;
madwoman who has maddened me,
I love you as much as I hate you.

Often in the garden
through which I drag my torpor,
I have felt, like an irony,
the sun tear open my breast;

And the green and the spring
wounded my heart so deeply
that I punished upon a flower
Nature’s insolence.

So, one night, I would like,
when the hour of pleasure comes,
to creep without a sound, like a coward,
toward the treasures that adorn you,

to punish your flesh,
to bruise your unpardoned breast,
and open in your astonished side
a long and deep wound,

And—dizzying sweetness!—
through those new lips,
more dazzling and more beautiful,
to inject my venom into you, my sister.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The poem’s disturbing fusion of desire, envy, and violence is preserved without softening.

title: The Fountain
text:
Your eyes are tired, poor lover!
Let them remain closed a long while,
in that indolent pose
in which pleasure surprised you.
The murmur of the fountain,
which endures by day and night,
gently prolongs the ecstasy
in which love immersed me.

        The ample jet,
        in a thousand flowers
        where Phoebe shows
        her colors,
        falls like a rain
        of slow tears.

Thus your soul, set ablaze
by the harsh light of joy,
darts bold and swift
toward enchanted skies.
Dying, it changes
into a sad, languid wave
that, down an invisible slope,
plunges into my heart.

        The ample jet,
        in a thousand flowers
        where Phoebe shows
        her colors,
        falls like a rain
        of slow tears.

O you, made beautiful by night,
how sweet it is, against your breast,
to hear the eternal moan
that sobs in the basin!
Water, sound, moon, night,
trees trembling all around,
your pure melancholy
is the mirror of my love.

        The ample jet,
        in a thousand flowers
        where Phoebe shows
        her colors,
        falls like a rain
        of slow tears.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The recurring fountain refrain and its visual indentation are retained.

title: Reversibility
text:
Angel filled with joy, do you know anguish,
guilt, shame, weariness, sobs,
and the vague terrors of those dreadful nights
that crush the heart like crumpled paper?
Angel filled with joy, do you know anguish?

Angel filled with goodness, do you know hatred,
tears of gall and clenched fists,
when vengeance raises its infernal voice
and sets itself up as captain of our faculties?
Angel filled with goodness, do you know hatred?

Angel filled with health, do you know Fever,
which, along the wall of the milky hospital,
walks with weary steps like the exiles,
seeking the scant sun and moving its lips?
Angel filled with health, do you know Fever?

Angel filled with beauty, do you know wrinkles,
and fear of growing old, and that hateful torment
of reading the secret horror of sacrifice
in eyes from which our own once drank?
Angel filled with beauty, do you know wrinkles?

Angel filled with happiness, light, and joy!
Dying David would have asked for healing
from the emanations of your bewitching body;
but from you, angel, I implore only prayers,
angel filled with happiness, light, and joy!
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. A stray source glyph following ‘David’ is treated as typographic noise.

title: Landscape
text:
To write my eclogues chastely, I wish
to sleep near heaven, as astrologers do,
and dreamily hear, close to the bells,
their solemn hymns borne abroad by winds.
Chin in my hands, peaceful in my garret,
I shall watch the workshop chatter and sing;
the chimneys, the steeples, those urban masts,
and skies that invite dreams of eternity.

It is sweet to see, emerging through the mist,
the star in the blue, the lamp in the window,
rivers of coal-smoke rising to the firmament,
and the moon pouring out her pallid spell.
I shall see the springs, the summers, the autumns;
and when winter comes with monotonous snows,
I shall seal fast shutters and screens
to raise my fairy palaces in the night.
Then I shall dream of blue horizons,
gardens, fountains lamenting in marble,
kisses and birds singing night and day,
and all that the Idyll holds of pure and childish.
The Riot, beating vainly at my panes,
will not make me lift my forehead from my desk,
for I shall be savoring the voluptuous joy
of summoning Spring at my will,
of raising a sun in my heart and making
a tender atmosphere from my burning thoughts.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The urban prospect and the poet’s inwardly created spring are preserved.

title: Deceptive Love
text:
When I see you pass, O my indolent beloved,
parading the weariness of your fathomless gaze,
suspending your step, so harmonious and slow,
while music sounds and is lost among the roofs;

When I see, in the glow of gaslight tinting it,
your brow haloed by a morbid charm,
where the last lights of sunset bring back dawn,
and your bewitching eyes, like those in a painting,

I tell myself: how beautiful she is! what strange freshness!
Memory, inlaid, heavy and regal tower,
crowns her; and her heart, crushed like a fruit,
and her body stand ready for the wisest love.

Are you a fruit whose autumn gives ripe flavors?
A funeral vase waiting to be filled with tears?
A perfume that makes one dream of perfumes far away,
a caressing cushion or a basket of flowers?

I know there are eyes awash in cruel melancholy
that conceal no precious secret,
beautiful cases without jewels, lockets without relics,
more empty and more distant, O heavens, than those two of yours.

But is it not enough that you are the subtlest appearance,
delighting a heart that flees the truth?
What does your stupidity or indifference matter?
I salute you, ornament or mask. I adore only your beauty.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The beloved’s beauty remains deliberately poised between depth and empty appearance.

title: The Vampire’s Metamorphosis
text:
Meanwhile the woman, writhing like a snake
among embers, from her strawberry mouth,
kneading her breasts against her rigid corset,
spoke these words steeped in musk:
“My lips are moist, and I know the art
of losing consciousness in the depths of a bed.
I dry every tear upon my triumphant breasts
and make old men laugh with childish laughter.
For whoever sees me unveiled and naked,
I replace the sun, the moon, the sky, the stars.
I am, my dear sage, so learned in delights,
whether I smother a man in my dreaded arms
or yield my breast to bites,
timid and wanton, fragile and robust,
that upon these covers fainting with emotion,
powerless angels would damn themselves for me.”

When she had sucked the marrow from my bones
and I turned languidly toward her
to return a kiss, I saw only
a sticky wineskin brimming with pus.
I closed both eyes in frozen terror,
and when I tried to open them to that brightness,
beside me, instead of the strong mannequin
that seemed to have stocked itself with my blood,
pieces of skeleton collided in confusion,
from which rose the squeaks of a weather vane
or a signboard at the end of an iron rod,
swayed by the wind on winter nights.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The erotic boast and abrupt bodily horror are rendered without euphemism.

title: Beatrice
text:
In ashen lands, greenless and scorched,
as I complained to Nature,
and the dagger of my mind, wandering at random,
slowly sharpened itself upon my heart,
a great dark cloud, born of a storm,
that housed a troop of vicious demons
like furious, cruel dwarfs,
turned then to stare coldly at me;
and, like travelers astonished by a madman,
I heard them laugh and whisper among themselves,
exchanging signs and knowing winks:

“Let us look at our leisure at this caricature,
this shade of Hamlet aping his pose,
hair in the wind, uncertain gaze.
Is it not truly pitiful to see such a reveler,
this scoundrel, idler, lazy actor,
who, because he plays his part with art,
expects, by singing of his woes, to interest
the eagle and the cricket, the brook and flowers,
and even us, authors of such columns,
by loudly declaiming his public tirades?”

I could have simply turned away
my sovereign head—my pride is high as mountains
and rules over demons and storm clouds—
had I not glimpsed among that filthy troop
—and this crime did not make the sun reel!—
the queen of my soul, she of the peerless gaze,
laughing with them at my dark affliction
and, in passing, offering them an obscene caress.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The theatrical mockery and the final betrayal by the speaker’s Beatrice are retained.

title: Morning Twilight
text:
Reveille sounded in every barracks,
and the morning wind put out the lamps.

It was the hour when swarms of evil dreams
smother adolescents on their pillows;
when, like a throbbing, bloodshot eye,
the lamp makes a red stain upon the day,
and the soul, beneath the weight of the sleeping body,
imitates the struggles of daylight and lamp.
Like a tearful face wiped by the breeze,
a tremor of fleeting things fills the air,
and men tire of writing and of love.

Here and there the houses begin to smoke;
the women of pleasure, eyelids livid,
lie open-mouthed in broken sleep;
the poor women, dragging their cold, thin breasts,
blow upon the embers and their fingers.
It is the hour when, wrapped in grime and cold,
women in labor feel their pains increase;
like a broken sob amid the welling blood,
the cockcrow tears the dark air;
an ocean of mist bathes the buildings,
and the dying, inside the hospitals,
breathe their last between uneven hiccups.
The libertines return, shattered by their work.

Shivering dawn, dressed in green and rose,
advanced slowly over the deserted Seine,
and somber Paris, rubbing its eyes,
grasped its tools, an old laborer.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The dawn sequence and its parallel scenes of exhaustion, labor, birth, and death are preserved.

title: Damned Women
text:
Like motionless beasts stretched upon the sand,
they turn their eyes toward the ocean horizon,
and their seeking feet and joined hands
have sweet faintings and bitter tremors.

Some, hearts that love confidences,
deep in the wood where the stream sings,
spell out the love of their timid puberty
and mark the tender trees upon the trunk;

Others, like sisters, walk grave and slow
through rocks filled with apparitions,
where Saint Anthony saw surge like lava
those temptations with naked breasts;

And there are some who, by the light of dripping resins,
in the now mute hollows of pagan caves,
call upon you to aid their howling fever,
O Bacchus, who lulls every anxiety!

And others, whose throats display scapulars,
who hide a whip beneath their long robes,
mingle, in lonely nights and shadowy groves,
the foam of pleasure with the tears of torture.

O virgins, O monsters, O demons, O martyrs,
spirits disdainful of all reality,
craving infinity, devout women, satyrs,
now taut with screams, now dissolved in tears,

You whom my soul pursued into such hell,
my sisters, I love and pity you
for your muffled sorrows, your insatiable thirst,
and the urns of love your breasts contain.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The poem’s address to women marked by desire, devotion, punishment, and social condemnation is retained.

title: The Voice
text:
My cradle stood beside the library,
a somber Babel where novel, science, fable—
everything, Greek dust or Latin ash—
mingled. I was tall as a folio.
Two voices spoke to me. One, insidious and firm:
“The Earth is a cake brimming with sweetness;
I can—and your pleasure will never end!—
forge you an appetite of equal vastness.”
And the other: “Come! O come travel through dreams,
far from the possible and the known.”
And this one sang like wind across the sands,
a phantom risen from no one knows where,
caressing the ear even as it frightens it.
I answered you: “Yes! Sweet voice!” From that moment
dates what may be called my wound
and my fate. Behind the panels
of immense existence, in the blackest abyss,
I see distinctly the strangest worlds,
and, an ecstatic victim of my clairvoyance,
I drag after me snakes that bite my heels.

And since that moment, like the prophets,
with immense tenderness I love the sea and desert;
I smile at funerals and sob at feasts,
and find a pleasant savor in the sourest wine;
facts sometimes seem lies to me,
and looking at the sky I fall into deep pits.
But the voice consoles me, saying: “The dreams
of madmen are more beautiful than those of the wise.”
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The source’s minor ‘de que parte’ typo is read in context as ‘de qué parte.’

title: Mœsta et Errabunda
text:
Does your heart not often flee, Agatha, far from you,
far from the black ocean of the filthy city,
toward another ocean where splendor suddenly bursts forth,
blue, profound, clear as virginity?
Does your heart not often flee, Agatha, far from you?

The sea, the boundless sea, consoles our toil!
What demon endowed the sea, that hoarse singer
seconded by the mighty organ of the winds,
with the sublime office of cradling our dreams?
The sea, the boundless sea, consoles our toil!

Carry me off, frigate! Drag me away, train!
Far away! Here tears have turned to mud!
Is it not true that Agatha’s heart often says:
Far from crimes, from pain and guilt,
carry me off, frigate! Drag me away, train!

How far away you are now, fragrant paradise,
where beneath the heavens all is love and laughter,
where what one loves is worthy of love,
where the heart drowns in pure delight!
How far away you are now, fragrant paradise!

But that paradise of youthful loves,
the races, songs, kisses, and flowers,
violins sounding behind the hills,
and jugs of wine at night in the thicket—
but that paradise of youthful loves,

Innocent paradise of furtive pleasures,
is it farther away than India and China?
Can we call it back with plaintive cries
and still revive it with a silvery voice,
that innocent paradise of furtive pleasures?
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The Latin title is retained, and the refrains and apostrophe to Agatha are preserved.

title: The Jewels
text:
She was naked and, knowing my tastes,
had kept only her sounding jewels,
whose ornaments lent her the conquering air
Moorish slave women wear on festive days.

When that radiant world of gems and metal
flings its mocking sound into the air,
it plunges me into ecstasy; I madly love
things in which sound and light unite.

She lay there and allowed herself to be loved,
smiling with happiness from the high divan
upon my passion, deep and slow as the sea,
which rose toward her as toward its cliff.

Her eyes fixed upon me as upon a tamed tiger,
she dreamily tried different poses,
and candor joined to lechery
added new grace to her metamorphoses;

And her arms and legs, her thighs and flanks,
polished as oil, undulant as a swan,
passed before my lucid, tranquil eyes;
and her belly and breasts, clusters of my vine,

advanced, as warm as Angels of evil,
to trouble the peace in which my soul lay
and wrench it from the crystal rock
where it had settled, solitary and serene.

And I thought I saw united in a new design
—so greatly did her waist throw her pelvis into relief—
the hips of Antiope with the torso of a youth;
how superb the makeup upon her dark skin!

And when the lamp had resigned itself to die,
since the fire alone lit the room,
each time it breathed out a flaming flash
it flooded her amber-colored skin with blood.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The erotic gaze, art-historical allusion, and changing firelight are retained.

title: The Fool and the Venus
text:
What an admirable day! The vast park swoons beneath the Sun’s burning gaze, as youth does beneath the dominion of Love.

The universal ecstasy of things is expressed by no sound; the very waters seem asleep. So unlike human festivities, this is a silent orgy.

One might say that an ever-increasing light gives things an ever-brighter glitter; that the excited flowers burn with desire to rival the blue of the sky through the force of their colors; and that the heat, making perfumes visible, lifts them toward the star like smoke.

But amid the universal joy I have seen one afflicted being.

At the feet of a colossal Venus, one of those artificial fools, one of those voluntary jesters charged with making kings laugh when remorse or weariness obsesses them, decked out in a brilliant and ridiculous costume, wearing horns and bells, crouches beside the pedestal and raises tear-filled eyes toward the immortal goddess.

And his eyes say: “I am the last and loneliest of human beings, deprived of love and friendship; I am far below the most imperfect animal. Yet I too was made to understand and feel immortal beauty. Alas, Goddess! Have pity on my sadness and my delirium!”

But the implacable Venus gazes far away at I know not what with her marble eyes.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The prose paragraphs and the contrast between universal ecstasy and the fool’s exclusion are preserved.

title: Draft Epilogue
text:
Calm as a sage, meek as one accursed, I said:

I love you, O my beauty, my enchantress…

How many times…

Your thirstless orgies, your soulless loves,
your taste for the infinite
proclaimed in everything, even evil,

Your bombs, your daggers, your victories, your festivals,
your melancholy neighborhoods,
your sumptuous hotels,
your gardens filled with intrigues and sighs,
your temples vomiting musical prayers,
your childish tantrums, your games of a mad old woman,
your despondencies;

Your fireworks, eruptions of joy
that make the dark and silent sky laugh.

Your venerable vice, flaunted in silk,
and your laughable virtue, with its unhappy
and gentle gaze, enraptured by the luxury it displays…

Your rescued principles, your vulnerable laws,
your high monuments where mist hangs,
your metal towers glittering in the sun,
your queens of the stage with enchanting voices,
your alarm bells, your deafening cannon,
your magic paving stones that raise fortresses,

Your paltry orators with baroque manners,
preaching love, and your sewers, brimming with blood,

Sinking into Hell like Orinocos.

Your fools, your angels, new in their tinsel.
Angels clad in gold, hyacinth, and purple,
bear witness that I fulfilled my duty
like a perfect chemist, like a devout soul.

For from each thing I drew its quintessence:—

You gave me your mud and I turned it into gold.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The draft’s fragmentary opening, catalog of the city, and alchemical close are retained.

title: The Denial of Saint Peter
text:
Indeed, what does God do with that sea of curses
that rises every day toward his seraphim?
Like a despot sated with food and wine,
he falls asleep to the sweet sound of our blasphemies.

The lamentations of martyrs and the tortured
are surely an intoxicating symphony,
since, despite the blood their delight costs,
the heavens still do not seem sated!

Remember, Jesus, that Garden of Olives!
In utter simplicity you prayed on your knees
to him who, in his heaven, laughed at the nails
base executioners drove into your flesh,

When you saw the rabble of guardroom and kitchen
spit upon your divinity,
and when you felt the thorns pierce
your head where humankind had dwelt,

When the dreadful weight of your broken body
stretched your straining arms, and your blood
and sweat ran down your pale brow,
when you were displayed as a target before all,

Did you remember the brilliant, lovely days
when you came to fulfill the eternal promise,
when astride a gentle she-ass you traveled
roads strewn with flowers and branches,

When, your breast swollen with hope and courage,
you forcefully scourged the vile merchants,
when you were master? Did repentance not pierce
your side more deeply than the spear?

As for me, I shall surely leave satisfied
a world where action is no sister to the dream;
may I kill by the sword and die by the sword!
Saint Peter denied Jesus… he did well!
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The poem’s blasphemous challenge and final endorsement of Peter’s denial are preserved.

title: Confession
text:
Once, one time only, sweet and gentle woman,
        your polished arm rested in mine
(and against the dark depths of my soul
        that memory has not faded);

It was late; like a newly minted medal,
        the full Moon appeared,
and the solemnity of night, like a river,
        spread over sleeping Paris.

Cats beneath the carriage gates
        slipped furtively,
ears alert, or, like dear shadows,
        followed us slowly.

And suddenly, amid that intimacy
        opened in the pale light,
from you, rich and resonant instrument in which
        the brightest joy vibrates,

From you, clear and merry as a fanfare
        in the sparkling morning,
a plaintive note, a strange note,
        escaped uncertainly,

Like a sullen child, horrible and sick,
        who would shame its family,
and whom, for years, to hide it from the world,
        they had locked inside a cellar.

Your discordant note, my poor angel, sang:
        “That nothing here below is firm,
and that always, however much it disguises itself,
        human selfishness betrays itself;

That being a beautiful woman is a hard trade
        and is rather the banal labor
of the mad, frozen dancer fixed
        in a mechanical smile;

That trusting hearts is very stupid;
        that everything—beauty and love—is a snare,
and in the end Oblivion tosses them in a basket
        and returns them to Eternity!”

I have often recalled that enchanted moon,
        that silence and that languor,
and that painful confidence, whispered
        by the heart in its confessional.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The alternating indentation and the beloved’s dissonant confession are preserved.

title: The Clock
text:
The Chinese see the hour in cats’ eyes. One day, a missionary walking through a suburb of Nanking noticed that he had forgotten his watch and asked a little boy what time it was.

The child of the Celestial Empire hesitated at first; then, collecting himself, he answered: “I shall tell you.” A few moments later he reappeared carrying a large cat, and, looking into what is commonly called the whites of its eyes, declared without hesitation: “It is not yet exactly noon.” And so it was.

As for me, if I lean toward the beautiful feline, so aptly named, who is at once an honor to her sex, the pride of my heart, and the perfume of my spirit, whether by night or day, in light or opaque shadow, in the depths of her adorable eyes I always see the hour clearly, always the same: an hour vast, solemn, immense as space, without divisions of minutes or seconds, a motionless hour unmarked by clocks, and yet light as a sigh, swift as a glance.

If some tiresome person came to disturb me while my gaze rested on so delicious a sphere; if some evil and intolerant spirit, some Demon of untimeliness, came to say: “What are you looking at so carefully? What do you seek in that creature’s eyes? Do you see the hour there, prodigal and idle mortal?” I would answer without hesitation: “Yes, I see the hour in them. It is Eternity!”

Is it not true, madam, that this is a truly meritorious madrigal and as emphatic as you yourself? Indeed, I have taken so much pleasure in embroidering this presumptuous gallantry that I shall ask nothing of you in return.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The prose-poem structure, Nanking anecdote, and mock-gallant conclusion are retained.

title: A Hemisphere in a Head of Hair
text:
Let me breathe for a long, long time the scent of your hair; let me plunge my face into it like a thirsty man into spring water, and wave it with my hand like a fragrant handkerchief, to shake memories into the air.

If you could know all I see! All I feel! All I hear in your hair! My soul travels through perfume as other men’s souls travel through music.

Your hair contains an entire dream, full of sails and masts; it contains vast seas whose monsoons carry me toward enchanting climates where space is bluer and deeper, where the air is perfumed by fruit, leaves, and human skin.

In the ocean of your hair I glimpse a harbor teeming with melancholy songs, vigorous men of every nation, and ships of every shape, their fine and intricate architectures outlined against an immense sky where eternal heat lounges at ease.

In the caresses of your hair I find again the languors of long hours spent on a divan in the cabin of a beautiful ship, rocked by the harbor’s imperceptible sway, among flowerpots and cooling jars.

In the glowing hearth of your hair I breathe the odor of tobacco mingled with opium and sugar; in the night of your hair I see the infinity of tropical blue shine; on the downy shores of your hair I grow drunk on the combined scents of cotton, musk, and coconut oil.

Let me bite your heavy black braids for a long time. When I nibble your elastic, rebellious hair, it seems to me that I am eating memories.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The repeated synesthetic voyages through scent, sound, sight, and touch are preserved.
